home.title: goflag: a CLI that flags invisible site defects in CI
home.description: A CLI that reports broken links, missing translation pages, a robots.txt that contradicts your pages, and misconfigured SEO metadata. JSON-first, MIT.

hero.title: Your page is perfect. Google no longer sees it.
hero.lead: goflag is a CLI that reads your site the way a crawler does, and fails a CI step before an invisible defect ships.

terminal.title: The whole interface
terminal.lead: The JSON report is the interface: pipe it into scripts, diff it between runs, gate CI on it, or hand it to an AI agent. The terminal output is a render of it.
terminal.caption: Real output; only the spacing is adjusted for the page. Progress goes to stderr so stdout stays clean for the report.

invisible.title: What a browser cannot show you
invisible.lead: Each of these renders perfectly. The defect is in the part of the page nobody looks at, and the cost is paid in a search index you never see.

one.see: A page that renders exactly as designed.
one.consequence: The page asks to be dropped in favour of another. It will be.

two.see: Four locales, every one of them reachable.
two.consequence: Each translation competes with the other three instead of consolidating with them.

three.see: A live production site, serving traffic.
three.consequence: No page is ever fetched, so the index directive on every page is never read.

method.title: Gate on regressions, not on perfection
method.lead: A run that fails on any finding is unusable on a site that is not clean yet, so it gets switched off, or quietly ignored. Three flags make the gate tenable, and one of them makes the backlog actually shrink.

step1.title: Capture a baseline
step1.body: Freeze today’s findings as known, so the gate can ask whether this change made things worse instead of whether the site is perfect. The output never says clean while findings are outstanding; it says how many are being let through.

step2.title: Gate on what is new
step2.body: Findings are matched by fingerprint, and page URLs are normalised to origin-independent routes, so a baseline captured against production compares cleanly with a run against localhost.

step3.title: Lower the ratchet
step3.body: Fix a finding, drop --max-debt by one, commit both. Without this, a baseline fossilises behind a build that passes.

ci.title: In CI
ci.lead: Two moments are worth auditing, and they answer different questions.
ci.mrAgainst: The branch’s own build, booted by --start
ci.deployAnswers: Is what is actually serving correct?
ci.detail: The flags worth knowing (--no-external, version pinning, exit codes) are three short sections in the docs.

proof.title: Built by auditing my own sites
proof.lead: goflag exists because four sites I run needed it, this one included: goflag.tech is gated by its own audit in CI, and a merge that breaks it does not land. Every number below is measured, not estimated.

not.title: What goflag is not
not.closing: One command, a JSON report, an exit code. If what you want is a number to optimise, this is the wrong tool: a score invites optimising the score.
not.versus: If you want a desktop crawler with a UI, Screaming Frog exists; if you only want dead links, lychee is faster. goflag is for gating a build on what a crawler reads.

source.q: Does it need access to my source code?
source.a: No. It needs a URL. goflag reads what a crawler reads, which is also why it catches things a local build cannot show you: the real base URL, whatever the proxy serves for robots.txt, the redirects.

next.a: The checks do: they judge HTML, and HTML is HTML. The fix snippets attached to findings assume the Next.js App Router, and say so. Nothing breaks on a Rails or Astro site; you just get the finding without the copy-paste remedy.

remedy.q: Can it fix what it finds?
remedy.a: Not on your site: it reads what a crawler reads and never touches your source. But the same project ships @goflag/next, a route registry for the Next.js App Router that produces the metadata, the hreflang cluster, the sitemap and robots.txt from one declaration, so several of these findings stop being possible. It is documented under The Next.js library.

chromium.a: Only without --static. A page whose head looks empty is re-rendered in headless Chromium, so a client-rendered app is not reported as missing everything; --static turns that off and never downloads a browser.

privacy.a: The HTTP requests to the site you named, and nothing else. The report is written to your disk or your stdout.

scale.q: Will it finish on a large site?
scale.a: The largest site it gates is {pages} pages and takes about {duration} with --static --no-external. --max-pages caps the crawl, --include and --exclude narrow it, and a run that hit a cap says so in diagnostics rather than reporting a smaller number as if it were the whole site.

close.title: Point it at your site.
close.lead: The quickstart takes you from a red first run to a gate you trust.

notFound.lead: This page does not exist. If a link on this site brought you here, that is a broken link, and there is a tool for that.
notFound.irony: Yes, the irony is noted. The site is audited by goflag in its own pipeline; a 404 reachable from a link would fail that build.
